title: Microsoft real-time media SDK
subtitle: A .NET 8 media service on Microsoft's real-time media SDK, handling unmanaged buffers on the SDK's clock and joined to a Linux voice engine across clouds.

stats.label: audio buffers through the soak, zero receive stalls and zero reconnects

media round trip on one probe

lede: Helix runs its speech models and conversation engine on Linux GPUs I own, and Microsoft Teams hands raw call audio only to a Windows application built on Microsoft's real-time media SDK. I refused to send call audio to a hosted AI service to avoid that mismatch, so I built a bridge and kept the brain at home. The bridge is a .NET 8 solution of six projects (host, calls, media, transport, contracts and unit tests) on a Microsoft Azure Windows machine. Its only job is media: join the call, receive and send audio frames, and publish the agent's screen as video.
quote: A colleague who answers a question from twenty seconds ago is worse than one who asks you to repeat it.
evidence: Microsoft Teams real-time media: a .NET 8 bridge on Microsoft's real-time media SDK that moved 91,643 audio buffers at 50.001 a second from Azure to Linux with zero receive stalls.
Real-time audio with unmanaged memory: buffers allocated and freed under the SDK's ownership rules, a paced 20-millisecond pump and bounded channels for back-pressure.
Failure testing for real-time systems: a forced mid-call reconnect inside the same call, 8,833 buffers with one 250 ms retry, and microphone audio from the break dropped.
Cross-language wire protocols: one authenticated WebSocket per call carrying a binary media protocol implemented in C# and Rust, tested byte for byte against shared golden vectors.
author: Corey James
